items.title: [zmescience.com] Protein evidence identifies Chinese fossils as Denisovans, revealing likely facial traits
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have identified human fossils from Xujiayao in northern China as Denisovans using ancient proteins, then compared their bones with other remains to infer the group’s likely appearance. The fossils suggest Denisovans had low, backward-sloping foreheads, heavy brow ridges and broad, relatively flat faces, with features distinct from those of Neanderthals. The team recovered a Denisovan-linked collagen variant from two fossils with no surviving DNA. The Xujiayao collection includes 20 specimens excavated decades ago. The researchers argue that some Chinese fossils previously assigned to separate human groups may instead represent variation within the Denisovan lineage. That classification remains uncertain for specimens identified only by resemblance, and researchers say additional samples would help test it.

items.title: [sciencenews.org] Ancient viral DNA silences chimp gene linked to early brain development
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers at Lund University report that DNA left by an ancient retrovirus, PTERV1, silences LINC00662, a gene active in human brain development, in chimpanzees. In lab-grown brain organoids, switching off the gene reduced the activity of genes involved in neuron development and connections; removing the viral sequence from chimpanzee stem cells restored LINC00662 activity. The researchers caution that the experiments cannot establish effects on whole-brain development, abilities or behavior. The study appeared in Science Advances on October 23. The team says it will investigate whether other viral remnants had similar effects and whether such sequences are linked to brain diseases.

Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height.

Roman’s Wide Field Instrument now produces image quality nearly 30% better than predicted, promising exceptionally sharp cosmic surveys.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says the strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and is nearly certain to persist until February 2027. The climate pattern, which warms the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is forecast to bring above-average temperatures across much of the world and shift rainfall patterns, increasing drought and flood risks in different regions. In Ecuador, the Navy’s Oceanographic and Antarctic Institute reported sea temperatures as much as 5.2°C above normal off Ecuador and Peru. It linked the unusually warm water to exceptional coastal rainfall, rainfall deficits in the Andean highlands and Amazon, and reduced nutrient levels affecting some fisheries. Officials urged preparations for coastal flooding. Separately, Copernicus reported that the global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached a September record of 21.05°C.

items.title: [bleepingcomputer.com] Hackers weaponize LiteLLM release to steal credentials across systems
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Hackers compromised the release pipeline for LiteLLM, an open-source AI gateway, and published version 1.107.0 containing credential-stealing malware on PyPI and Docker on Oct. 21. The malicious release affected Windows, Linux and macOS installations and targeted cloud, developer and AI-service credentials. The project says its private enterprise registry was not affected. LiteLLM said attackers used stolen GitHub CLI tokens to alter and trigger the release, apparently after accessing an internet-exposed internal deployment. It has not confirmed how they gained access. The compromised package has been removed. Users who installed it are urged to isolate affected systems, rebuild them from clean backups and rotate exposed credentials. Version 1.106.2 is the latest clean release.

items.title: [theguardian.com] French bond yields hit 24-year high as budget fears deepen
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

France’s 10-year government bond yield climbed to 5.1415% on Thursday, its highest since July 2002, while the premium over German bonds widened to 177.7 basis points, the largest since November 2011. Investors are demanding more compensation as political uncertainty, renewed street unrest and difficulty passing the 2027 budget weigh on the country’s fiscal outlook. The government has proposed €54 billion in spending cuts for 2027, but parliamentary divisions leave it unclear how much it can enact. France’s deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, and public debt stood at 115.6%. Foreign investors held nearly 55% of French government debt last year. Markets are watching Moody’s scheduled review of France’s Aa3 rating on Friday, Oct. 23, and the European Central Bank’s Oct. 29 rate decision. Analysts cited by Reuters said ECB support would require a much more severe, disorderly market disruption, not just higher borrowing costs.

Microsoft on Oct. 21 attributed the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain breach to Storm-0940, a China-aligned hacking group that used the ARTEX AI framework in a campaign targeting hundreds of organizations worldwide. The attackers used compromised ConnectWise application identities and permissions already granted to those apps to access customers' Microsoft 365 environments without an interactive user sign-in. Microsoft said Storm-0940 attempted to access more than 2,250 tenants and, in several cases, gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after selecting a target. ARTEX automated scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and abuse of application permissions. ConnectWise said Oct. 22 that it was restoring services in phases over several days and told customers to keep affected connections disabled until they receive service-specific instructions. The company said its existing backup archives remained encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication they were compromised.

items.title: [MacRumors] Apple Ordered to Open iPhone to Rival App Stores in Australia
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Australia's Federal Court today ordered Apple to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads, and alternative payment services for Australian users from March 1, 2027.


The orders follow the court's August 2025 finding that Apple misused its market power by restricting app distribution and payment options. They cover users whose Apple Account region is Australia, with Apple Developer Program members worldwide able to participate.

Apple must let users find, download, install, and update apps through competing marketplaces and websites without charging for access or obstructing their use. Developers must receive the necessary tools on substantially the same terms as for App Store distribution, and Apple cannot penalize them for using competing stores or payment services.

Developers will also be able to offer alternative payments and link to other ways to pay, including within ‌App Store‌ apps. Apple cannot require them to offer its own purchasing system alongside alternatives, report those transactions, or allow Apple to audit them. Developers can offer lower prices through competing payment services without Apple preventing them.

The ruling also limits Apple's ability to collect fees on those purchases. It cannot charge for purchases through alternative payment services or websites in apps distributed outside the ‌App Store‌. For ‌App Store‌ apps, fees are capped at the equivalent charge for payments for physical goods or services, plus any genuine, reasonable additional costs Apple incurs for digital purchases.

Apple also cannot make alternative distribution conditional on developers offering content purchased elsewhere through its own payment system.

Security checks will remain. Apps downloaded outside the ‌App Store‌ must undergo an automated security or privacy scan and be notarized by Apple or a qualified third party. However, Apple cannot impose disproportionate installation barriers or otherwise obstruct alternative distribution. Additional security requirements for competing payments must be necessary and proportionate, with developers given an explanation in advance.

Apple can remove or disable externally installed apps only in specified cases involving harmful content, genuine security risks, or legal requirements. It cannot ban third-party apps or alternative app stores from being preinstalled on iPhones, but does not have to distribute competing stores through the ‌App Store‌.

Apple told Reuters that it plans to appeal the ruling and ask the court to pause its enforcement, citing its intellectual property rights and ‌App Store‌ security.

The changes take effect at noon Melbourne time on March 1, 2027. Apple can apply between February 1 and February 15, with supporting evidence, for a court-approved extension until May 3.

items.title: [farmer.pl] Farmers urged to shred corn stalks to curb pests and disease
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

As Poland’s corn harvest continues, agronomic guidance recommends finely shredding stalks and other crop residues after harvest to reduce winter shelter for the European corn borer and limit disease in the next season. The borer’s larvae overwinter in stalks, while feeding damage can promote Fusarium infections that contaminate grain with mycotoxins. Residue management also affects soil organic matter: grain corn leaves substantial biomass in the field, while silage harvesting removes nearly all above-ground material. Guidance recommends accounting for soil moisture and the next crop; working wet soil can cause compaction, and fields vulnerable to erosion may need residue left on the surface.

items.title: [Fast Company] AI chatbots struggle to understand cultural context, a new study finds
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

AI models often struggle to understand cultures around the world, and are reluctant to admit when they don’t know something. That’s what researchers at Canadian AI lab Cohere Labs found when they tested whether chatbots could do more than simply speak a culture’s language. To determine whether models possessed deeper cultural knowledge, they presented them with a series of unique cultural riddles.

Here’s one of them: “What’s the German 9/11?” Out of 28 AI models, only one knew the answer. The models were likely thrown off by the date format (seven answered “the twin towers”). In Europe, the day comes first, then the month, so 9/11 is November 9, the day in 1989 when the Berlin Wall fell.

Many existing AI benchmarks assess cultural knowledge, from everyday breakfast foods and historical events to traditional holiday customs. They often treat culture as a collection of static facts, things you can memorize or look up with a quick web search. But knowing facts about a culture isn’t the same as understanding how people within it make sense of the world. The researchers knew they needed a test that asked models to connect seemingly unrelated pieces of cultural knowledge and put them to use. That’s what led them to riddles, and to a different kind of cultural benchmark that called for answers rooted in lived experience.

“This is something that we’re trying to capture with this benchmark—these little nuances, these little hard-to-capture fuzzy concepts that are not as easy to verify . . . This is where the real-life complexity gets in,” says Julia Kreutzer, a staff research scientist at Cohere Labs, who led the development of the “CulturalRiddles” benchmark.

Kreutzer and her team spent six months working with volunteers around the world to collect riddles, put them to AI models, and evaluate their answers. The researchers also used those expert evaluations to tune and validate an AI model that could judge the quality of answers where expert assessments were missing.

In all, Cohere Labs researchers tested 28 AI models on cultural riddles written by 166 volunteers from 45 countries in 51 languages. The volunteers evaluated and labeled 68,154 unique answers from the models. Researchers then ranked the models based on their overall accuracy across the languages and cultures tested.

The results

Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview earned the highest score, at 79.4%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 placed second at 76.3%, followed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking at 66%.

Alibaba’s Qwen 3.5 0.8B claimed the dubious honor of finishing last, answering just 0.4% of the riddles correctly. Other notable performers included Amazon’s Nova Micro, which got just 8.3% of the riddles right, and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, which scored 33.6%.

Even the best-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, scored below 50% accuracy in 6 of the 57 communities tested, underscoring how much ground the industry still has to cover on cultural awareness.

More troublingly, the benchmark revealed that models were far more likely to guess at an answer than admit they didn’t know. Even when explicitly told they could answer “I don’t know,” models did so just 0.7% of the time. About 31% of the answers reviewers checked were simply made up, with varying degrees of creativity.

“They would confidently answer and sometimes that’s ridiculous and funny,” Kreutzer says, “but sometimes it can also get really offensive and you can see the models defaulting to more dominant cultures on the web, instead of answering with local grounding.”

Cohere Labs conducted a separate survey to explore how AI’s cultural knowledge gaps play out in practice. Many chatbot users around the world said they have to switch to English to get useful responses because answers generated in their own languages aren’t helpful. Users described responses that miss crucial cultural context and, in some cases, AI systems that run afoul of their cultural norms.

The Cohere Labs researchers concluded that cultural awareness needs to be built into AI models from the ground up if the tools they power are going to serve everyone, not just cultures already well represented in the training data. And their CulturalRiddles benchmark suggests that many of today’s models still fall short.

Kreutzer and her team designed CulturalRiddles to keep growing. They open-sourced the riddles, code, demo, and interactive dashboard so that anyone can contribute riddles from their own culture through a review process.

“Ideally this benchmark will get adopted not only by academic researchers but also by big industry labs who are trying to show we’re advancing the state of the art, not only in very verifiable hard tasks but also in the softer tasks,” Kreutzer says.

Researchers using artificial intelligence uncovered two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language used by about 70% of websites. Security updates were released on Oct. 21. The flaws could let attackers run malicious code on affected servers without logging in, potentially stealing data or disrupting websites. Organizations rushed to patch systems, while some government and private websites were temporarily taken offline as a precaution. Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince said attempts to exploit the flaws rose from thousands before public disclosure to tens of thousands within 45 minutes, hundreds of thousands within two hours and millions afterward. The PHP Foundation said Chainguard broke an embargo before the fix was ready, while Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc said he believed the flaw was already being exploited. Security agencies urged operators to install patches, and researchers cautioned that attempts to exploit a flaw do not necessarily mean attackers have working tools.
